content: 1. Before the age of 18, many individuals experience sexual abuse. Both sexual violence and intimate partner violence are predominantly perpetrated by men and boys against women and girls. However, men and boys, though less commonly, can also be victims of gender-based violence. Adolescent girls are particularly vulnerable to sexual violence and abuse. 2. Nearly one in four married or partnered adolescent girls aged 15–19 years is subjected to physical and/or sexual violence by a husband or partner. Intimate partner violence disproportionately affects adolescent girls in lowand lower-middle-income countries and regions. The disparity between highand lower-income regions is especially pronounced for partner violence within the past 12 months, reflecting challenges in leaving abusive relationships in resource-constrained settings and where stigma levels are high. 3. Children with disabilities are at nearly three times greater risk of experiencing sexual violence compared to their non-disabled peers. Adolescent girls with disabilities face the highest risk during adolescence. They may also be subjected to forced sterilization, contraception, or abortion at the request of family members or healthcare professionals. These procedures are often justified under claims of medical necessity or best interest, but they are considered acts of violence under human rights frameworks. Girls with intellectual or psychosocial disabilities and/or those living in residential institutions are at the greatest risk of such violence. 4. Sexual violence can result in multiple burdens, including physical injuries, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), unintended pregnancies, emotional distress (e.g., fear, anger, self-blame, shame, sadness, or guilt), anxiety disorders (e.g., post-traumatic stress disorder), depression, medically unexplained somatic complaints, substance use disorders, and suicidal ideation or self-harm. Social trauma, including stigma, can lead to social exclusion, discrimination, and rejection by family and community. 5. Female genital mutilation (FGM) involves the partial or total removal of external genitalia or other injury to female genital organs for non-medical reasons. FGM has no health benefits and, instead, causes harm by interfering with the natural functioning of the body, leading to immediate and long-term health consequences. FGM is mostly performed on girls between birth and age 15 and is prevalent in 30 countries in Africa, as well as in parts of Asia and the Middle East. Due to international migration, FGM is now present globally. 6. Globally, 7 million adolescents aged 10–19 years were living with HIV in 2022, with adolescent girls accounting for 54% of the total. An estimated 140,000 adolescents were newly infected with HIV, three-quarters of whom were girls. Only about 65% of adolescents living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 2022, compared to 77% ART coverage among adults aged 15 years and older. Factors such as age-disparate sex, low condom use, sexual violence, coercion, gender norms, and early sexual debut contribute to the disproportionate risk of adolescent females acquiring HIV. 7. In 2022, an estimated 27,000 adolescents worldwide died from AIDS-related causes, with East and Southern Africa recording the highest number of deaths (16,000 among those aged 10–19 years). Stigma, discrimination, punitive laws and policies, violence, and entrenched societal and gender inequalities continue to hinder access to HIV prevention and treatment for adolescents. 8. The incidence of other STIs among adolescents was 7,089 per 100,000 population in 2019, with the highest incidence among young adolescents aged 10–14 years. Sexually active adolescents are at higher risk of acquiring STIs due to increased exposure, biological susceptibility, and limited access to or use of health services. For example, the peak time for acquiring infections like human papillomavirus (HPV) or herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2) is shortly after becoming sexually active, typically during adolescence. Vaccination against HPV and screening and treatment of precancerous lesions are cost-effective ways to prevent cervical cancer. 9. Five of the top 10 causes of death among adolescents are communicable diseases, including HIV/AIDS, diarrheal diseases, tuberculosis (TB), lower respiratory infections, and meningitis. In 2019, these diseases accounted for over 200,000 adolescent deaths globally. Diarrheal diseases, for instance, were the leading cause of death among young adolescent girls and the second leading cause among young adolescent boys. 10. Lower respiratory infections, such as influenza, pneumococcal pneumonia, and Haemophilus influenzae type b, were a major cause of adolescent deaths globally in 2019. Young adolescents accounted for nearly two-thirds of the approximately 32,000 associated deaths. Tuberculosis (TB) was the third leading cause of death among adolescents, with an estimated 71,000 deaths in 2019. Risk factors for TB include undernutrition, HIV infection, alcohol use, smoking, and diabetes. 11. Meningitis was the ninth leading cause of death among adolescents in 2019, with nearly 22,000 deaths globally. Approximately 70% of these deaths occurred in African lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Meningococcal meningitis remains a significant public health burden, particularly in the Meningitis Belt of Africa. 12. Adolescents have been significantly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, not through direct morbidity or mortality, but through the impact of pandemic response measures such as school closures, lockdowns, mobility restrictions, and service disruptions. These measures have exacerbated existing gender and age inequalities and increased ageand gender-based violence. 13. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as mental health conditions, cancers, skin diseases, migraines, asthma, and sensory impairments, are significant contributors to adolescent morbidity. Mental health conditions, including anxiety and depressive disorders, are among the leading causes of illness and disability in adolescents. Social, family, and individual factors, as well as the maturing brain's susceptibility to external influences, play a role in adolescent mental health. 14. Skin diseases, including dermatitis, psoriasis, scabies, fungal and viral infections, and acne, are a major cause of adolescent morbidity. Acne, nearly universal among adolescents, can range from mild to severe and cause emotional distress and physical scarring. 15. Migraines, a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent headaches, were the fourth leading cause of adolescent morbidity in 2019. Females had a migraine-related morbidity rate twice that of males. 16. Asthma, a chronic respiratory disease, ranked 12th as a cause of adolescent morbidity globally in 2019. Diagnosis and treatment of asthma remain challenging, particularly in LMICs, where under-diagnosis and inappropriate treatment often lead to uncontrolled symptoms. 17. Congenital anomalies, such as neural tube defects, heart anomalies, and Down syndrome, caused an estimated 20,000 adolescent deaths in 2019 and were the 10th leading cause of death. These conditions also contribute significantly to adolescent morbidity. 18. Sensory impairments, particularly vision and hearing impairments, significantly impact adolescents' communication, learning, social functioning, cognitive abilities, and quality of life. Myopia is the leading cause of vision impairment among children and adolescents, while exposure to loud sounds is a common cause of hearing loss. 19. Oral health issues, such as untreated dental caries, can lead to pain, chewing and sleeping difficulties, and reduced quality of life. Limited access to oral health services and high out-of-pocket costs often delay care. 20. Addressing the broader determinants of adolescent health, including social, economic, and environmental factors, requires multisectoral action and accountability.
